title: Demonstrationes circa residua ex divisione potestatum per numeros primos resultantia

deep.reconstruction:
Setting: p is a prime ≡ 1 (mod 4), written p = 4n+1, and a is a primitive root mod p. The fourth-power residues are the n classes a^{4k}.

(End of Coroll. 3) We have a^{2n} ≡ −1. This is a fourth power iff 2n ≡ 0 (mod 4), i.e. iff n is even, i.e. iff p ≡ 1 (mod 8). So for p ≡ 1 (mod 8), −1 is a biquadratic residue and the set of biquadratic residues is closed under negation. For p ≡ 5 (mod 8), −1 is a biquadratic non-residue.

Coroll. 4. Take b with p ∤ b.
- If p ≡ 1 (mod 8), the congruence u^4 ≡ −1 has exactly four solutions u. Choosing p' ≡ u·b gives b^4 + p'^4 ≡ 0 (mod p). So there are four such roots p' below the divisor.
- If p ≡ 5 (mod 8), b^4 + p'^4 ≡ 0 would force (p'/b)^4 ≡ −1, which is impossible. So no sum of two biquadrates prime to p is divisible by p.

Scholion 85. Euler uses two identities:
- b^4 + p^4 = (b² − p²)² + 2(bp)²
- b^4 + p^4 = (b² + p²)² − 2(bp)²
When p | b^4 + p'^4 with p ∤ bp', these give ±2·(bp)² ≡ (square) mod p. Hence both 2 and −2 are quadratic residues mod p for p ≡ 1 (mod 8).

Therefore p divides some x² + 2y² with gcd(x, y) = 1 and p ∤ y. Euler then invokes the descent lemma that every divisor of such a primitive x² + 2y² is itself of the form x² + 2y². This yields Fermat's theorem: every prime p ≡ 1 (mod 8) has the form x² + 2y². Euler says this is the first proof he has managed to find.

It also gives, as a by-product, the part p ≡ 1 (mod 8) of the second supplement to quadratic reciprocity, (2/p) = (−2/p) = 1. The next page notes that the case 8m+3 cannot be reached this way. It gives a descent proof communicated by a friend about divisors of 2p² − q².
errors: Minor gap in Coroll. 4: the statement 'no sum of two biquadrates is divisible by p' for p ≡ 5 (mod 8) needs the tacit restriction that b and p' are prime to the divisor; trivially p | p^4 + p^4.
The Scholion relies on the lemma about divisors of x² + 2y² (cited only as 'demonstrari possit'); it is not proved here.
Numbering slip: the Scholion is numbered 85, and the Theorema on the next page is also numbered 85.

ideas.what: −1 is a fourth-power residue mod p iff p ≡ 1 (mod 8); biquadratic residues are closed under negation exactly then
ideas.modern_name: Criterion for −1 to be a quartic residue (character of −1 in the quartic residue symbol)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler (E449 and related residue papers); later Gauss in his biquadratic residue theory

ideas.what: p ≡ 1 (mod 8) divides b^4 + c^4 with p ∤ bc; impossible for p ≡ 5 (mod 8)
ideas.modern_name: Solvability of x^4 ≡ −1 mod p (8th roots of unity mod p)

ideas.what: Identities b^4 + p^4 = (b² ∓ p²)² ± 2(bp)², used to show ±2 are quadratic residues for p ≡ 1 (mod 8), then descent to get p = x² + 2y²
ideas.modern_name: Proof of Fermat's x² + 2y² theorem for p ≡ 1 (mod 8); partial second supplementary law (2/p) = 1
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler (E449); the full theorem is usually credited to Euler and Lagrange
ideas.where_published: E449 §85; discussed in Weil, Number Theory: An Approach through History; Lemmermeyer, Reciprocity Laws (historical notes)

ideas.what: Divisors of primitive x² + 2y² are again of the form x² + 2y²
ideas.modern_name: Descent lemma for the principal form of discriminant −8
ideas.where_published: Euler's earlier papers on divisors of quadratic forms (exact location unsure); Lagrange, Recherches d'arithmétique (1773–75)

deep.surprise_reason: This is the well-known passage in which Euler first proves Fermat's claim for p ≡ 1 (mod 8) via biquadratic residues. It is documented in the standard histories (Weil, Lemmermeyer). Nothing on the page appears to be unrecognized.
transcription_corrections: Transcription is essentially accurate. The scan shows 'diuiſor primus fit formae 8m+1' partially struck through or overprinted by a line in Coroll. 4, but the text is as transcribed.
